claim: Gish was specifically purified by Ex1-468 in AP-MS experiments.
source: Upon re-analysis of our AP-MS data, we observed that Gilgamesh (Gish), the Drosophila orthologue of Casein kinase 1γ, was specifically purified by an Ex truncation that fully recapitulates the Crb-mediated effect on Ex stability (Ex1-468) (Figure 1A) (Ribeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS experimental data presented in Figure 1A and references a previous publication.

claim: Gish peptides were detected in Ex1-468 AP-MS only upon co-expression with wild-type Crb but not with CrbΔFBM.
source: Importantly, Gish peptides were detected in the Ex1-468 AP-MS only upon co-expression with wild-type (wt) Crb but not with a FERM-binding motif mutant version of Crb (ΔFBM) that cannot bind Ex or promote its depletion (Figure 1A) (Ling et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2010; Ribeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data shown in Figure 1A and cites previous publications demonstrating that CrbΔFBM cannot bind Ex.

claim: Hpo interacted with Ex regardless of Crb presence.
source: In contrast, Hpo interacted with Ex regardless of Crb presence, in agreement with previous reports (Figure 1A) (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data in Figure 1A and cites a previous publication.

claim: Crbintra promotes Ex:Gish binding in a FBM-dependent manner.
source: Crbintra promotes Ex:Gish binding in a FBM-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is stated in the figure legend and supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: An interaction between Gish and Ex1-468 was readily detected in S2 cells, specifically in the presence of wt Crb.
source: In reciprocal co-IP experiments, an interaction between Gish and Ex1-468 was readily detected in S2 cells, specifically in the presence of wt Crb (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP experimental data shown in Figures 1B-C.

claim: Only GishisoI, but not GishisoF, was able to interact with Ex.
source: Interestingly, only GishisoI, but not GishisoF, was able to interact with Ex (Figure 1B) suggesting that CKI sub-cellular localisation may be critical to the regulation of Ex.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data in Figure 1B and the authors infer that subcellular localization is important.

claim: CKI sub-cellular localisation may be critical to the regulation of Ex.
source: Interestingly, only GishisoI, but not GishisoF, was able to interact with Ex (Figure 1B) suggesting that CKI sub-cellular localisation may be critical to the regulation of Ex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only the palmitoylated isoform of Gish interacts with Ex.

claim: Co-expression of Ex1-468 and GishisoI in the absence of Crb resulted in a mild depletion of Ex1-468 protein levels.
source: Co-expression of Ex1-468 and GishisoI in the absence of Crb resulted in a mild depletion of Ex1-468 protein levels (Figure 2A), whereas GishisoF had no effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GishisoF had no effect on Ex1-468 protein levels.
source: Co-expression of Ex1-468 and GishisoI in the absence of Crb resulted in a mild depletion of Ex1-468 protein levels (Figure 2A), whereas GishisoF had no effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ex1-468 CAAX remains responsive to Crb.
source: Importantly, this variant remains responsive to Crb (Figure 2B), and co-immunoprecipitates with Gish in a Crb-dependent manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 1C.

claim: Ex1-468 CAAX co-immunoprecipitates with Gish in a Crb-dependent manner.
source: Importantly, this variant remains responsive to Crb (Figure 2B), and co-immunoprecipitates with Gish in a Crb-dependent manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ex1-468 CAAX ran mostly as a single band in S2 cells in the presence of CrbΔFBM.
source: Ex1-468 CAAX ran mostly as a single band in S2 cells in the presence of the CrbΔFBM mutant and, similar to wt Ex1-468, as a higher mobility band or doublet in the presence of wt Crb (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: Ex1-468 CAAX ran as a higher mobility band or doublet in the presence of wt Crb.
source: Ex1-468 CAAX ran mostly as a single band in S2 cells in the presence of the CrbΔFBM mutant and, similar to wt Ex1-468, as a higher mobility band or doublet in the presence of wt Crb (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: An electrophoretic mobility shift and depletion was observed when Ex1-468 CAAX was co-expressed with GishisoI, but not with a kinase-dead version of Gish (GishKD).
source: An electrophoretic mobility shift and depletion was also observed when Ex1-468 CAAX was co-expressed with GishisoI, but not with a kinase-dead version of Gish (GishKD) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Co-expression of Ex1-468 CAAX or full-length Ex with wt GishisoI, CkIα or Dco led to Ex mobility shift and depletion.
source: Indeed, co-expression of Ex1-468 CAAX or full-length (FL) Ex with wt GishisoI, CkIα or Dco led to Ex mobility shift and depletion, although their kinase-deficient (KD) versions did not (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Kinase-deficient versions of GishisoI, CkIα or Dco did not lead to Ex mobility shift and depletion.
source: Indeed, co-expression of Ex1-468 CAAX or full-length (FL) Ex with wt GishisoI, CkIα or Dco led to Ex mobility shift and depletion, although their kinase-deficient (KD) versions did not (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Multiple CKI family kinases can promote Ex phosphorylation and depletion.
source: Together, these results suggest that multiple CKI family kinases can promote Ex phosphorylation and depletion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that GishisoI, CkIα, and Dco all promote Ex mobility shift and depletion.

claim: All three CKI kinases (CkIα, Dco, GishisoI) readily promoted the degradation of wt Ex1-468 CAAX.
source: All three kinases readily promoted the degradation of wt Ex1-468 CAAX (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The S453A mutant levels were largely unaffected by CKI isoforms.
source: However, the S453A mutant levels were largely unaffected by CKI isoforms, consistent with the notion that the CKI-mediated regulation of Ex stability is dependent on the ability of Ex to interact with Slmb via the phosphodegron surrounding S453.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D and the authors infer the mechanism.

claim: CKI-mediated regulation of Ex stability is dependent on the ability of Ex to interact with Slmb via the phosphodegron surrounding S453.
source: However, the S453A mutant levels were largely unaffected by CKI isoforms, consistent with the notion that the CKI-mediated regulation of Ex stability is dependent on the ability of Ex to interact with Slmb via the phosphodegron surrounding S453.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutation of S453 prevents CKI-mediated Ex degradation.

claim: Expression of CkIα or GishisoI resulted in the appearance of a slower-migrating Ex1-468 S453A band.
source: Interestingly, expression of CkIα or GishisoI resulted in the appearance of a slower-migrating Ex1-468 S453A band (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There may be alternative CKI phosphorylation sites in Ex1-468 besides S453.
source: This suggests that, at least for CkIα and Gish, there may be alternative CKI phosphorylation sites in Ex1-468 besides S453.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CkIα and GishisoI cause a mobility shift in Ex1-468 S453A.

claim: GishisoI, but not GishisoF, promoted the interaction between Ex1-468 CAAX and Slmb in the absence of ectopic Crb.
source: We found that GishisoI, but not GishisoF, promoted the interaction between Ex1-468 CAAX and Slmb in the absence of ectopic Crb (Figure 2E), consistent with its ability to stimulate Ex mobility shift and depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CkIα and Dco were able to induce binding between Ex1-468 CAAX and Slmb in the absence of Crb.
source: CkIα and Dco were also able to induce binding between Ex1-468 CAAX and Slmb in the absence of Crb (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dco consistently showed a weaker effect on Ex phosphorylation than the other two kinases.
source: Dco consistently showed a weaker effect on Ex phosphorylation than the other two kinases.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from multiple experiments shown in the figures.

claim: An Ex truncation mutant lacking the domain containing the β-TrCP consensus motif (Ex1-450) was refractory to degradation and did not display a mobility shift following GishisoI expression.
source: Interestingly, an Ex truncation mutant lacking this domain (Ex1-450) was refractory to degradation, and did not display a mobility shift following GishisoI expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that CKIs act upstream of Slmb to promote Ex phosphorylation and degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and the authors infer the mechanism.

claim: CKIs act upstream of Slmb to promote Ex phosphorylation and degradation.
source: Interestingly, an Ex truncation mutant lacking this domain (Ex1-450) was refractory to degradation, and did not display a mobility shift following GishisoI expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that CKIs act upstream of Slmb to promote Ex phosphorylation and degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Ex1-450, which lacks the Slmb binding site, is not affected by CKI expression.

claim: Over-expression of Sgg did not promote Ex:Slmb binding.
source: However, we found that over-expression of Sgg did not promote Ex:Slmb binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of sgg did not abrogate Crb-induced Ex phosphorylation and degradation.
source: Moreover, RNAi-mediated depletion of sgg did not abrogate Crb-induced Ex phosphorylation and degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: CKI kinases, but not Sgg, regulate Ex phosphorylation and stability, acting upstream of Slmb/β-TrCP.
source: Together, our results indicate that the CKI kinases, but not Sgg, regulate Ex phosphorylation and stability, acting upstream of Slmb/β-TrCP.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple experiments showing CKI effects and lack of Sgg effects.

claim: The ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporters are normally localised at the apical cortex of wing imaginal disc cells.
source: As predicted, the ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporters resemble endogenous Ex in that they are normally localised at the apical cortex of wing imaginal disc cells (Figure 3A,B,D,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ubi-Ex1-468::GFP failed to localise to the apical surface in crb mutant tissue.
source: In agreement with previous observations of ExFL, ubi-Ex1-468::GFP failed to localise to the apical surface in crb mutant tissue (Figure 3A–A' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and accumulated at the apical cortex in slmb mutant clones (Figure 3B–B' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) (Chen et al., 2010; Hafezi et al., 2012; Ling et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2010; Ribeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A-A' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and cites previous publications.

claim: ubi-Ex1-468::GFP accumulated at the apical cortex in slmb mutant clones.
source: In agreement with previous observations of ExFL, ubi-Ex1-468::GFP failed to localise to the apical surface in crb mutant tissue (Figure 3A–A' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and accumulated at the apical cortex in slmb mutant clones (Figure 3B–B' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) (Chen et al., 2010; Hafezi et al., 2012; Ling et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2010; Ribeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B-B' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and cites previous publications.

claim: Loss of both crb and slmb led to accumulation of Ex1-468::GFP in the cytoplasm.
source: Loss of both crb and slmb led to accumulation of Ex1-468::GFP in the cytoplasm (Figure 3C–C'), suggesting that the Ex sensor can be degraded by SCFSlimb/β-TrCP in the cytoplasm, as had been suggested for endogenous Ex (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C-C' and cites a previous publication.

claim: The Ex sensor can be degraded by SCFSlimb/β-TrCP in the cytoplasm.
source: Loss of both crb and slmb led to accumulation of Ex1-468::GFP in the cytoplasm (Figure 3C–C'), suggesting that the Ex sensor can be degraded by SCFSlimb/β-TrCP in the cytoplasm, as had been suggested for endogenous Ex (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Ex1-468::GFP accumulates in the cytoplasm when both crb and slmb are lost, and cites a previous publication.

claim: When Crbintra was expressed in the posterior compartment using hh-Gal4, ubi-Ex1-468::GFP was lost from the apical surface and degraded.
source: When a Crbintra transgene was expressed in the posterior compartment using the hedgehog-Gal4 driver (hh-Gal4), ubi-Ex1-468::GFP was lost from the apical surface and degraded (Figure 3D–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The S453A mutant reporter accumulated upon Crbintra expression.
source: In contrast, the S453A mutant reporter accumulated upon Crbintra expression, presumably due to the fact that it cannot be recognised by Slmb and degraded (Figure 3F–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3F-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, and the authors infer the mechanism.

claim: Neither ubi-Ex1-468::GFP nor ubi-Ex1-468 S453A::GFP affected wing size when expressed at low levels under the control of the ubi promoter.
source: Indeed, neither reporter affected wing size when expressed at low levels under the control of the ubi promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing size measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-I.

claim: Expression of full-length Ex under the control of en-Gal4 driver induced a reduction in tissue size.
source: In contrast, expression of full-length Ex under the control of en-Gal4 driver induced a reduction in tissue size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J,L,P).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing size measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J,L,P.

claim: The tissue size reduction phenotype caused by full-length Ex expression was partially rescued by co-expression of Crbintra.
source: This phenotype was partially rescued by co-expression of Crbintra, which we expect would promote increased turnover and degradation of Ex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M,P).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing size measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1M,P and the authors infer the mechanism.

claim: Expression of the S453A mutant version of Ex resulted in a more severe undergrowth than wt Ex.
source: Interestingly, expression of the S453A mutant version of Ex resulted in a more severe undergrowth than wt Ex, and this was refractory to Crbintra co-expression, suggesting that Crb fails to regulate the levels of Ex when the residue that is recognised by Slmb/β-TrCP is mutated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing size measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N-P and the authors infer the mechanism.

claim: The S453A mutant Ex undergrowth phenotype was refractory to Crbintra co-expression.
source: Interestingly, expression of the S453A mutant version of Ex resulted in a more severe undergrowth than wt Ex, and this was refractory to Crbintra co-expression, suggesting that Crb fails to regulate the levels of Ex when the residue that is recognised by Slmb/β-TrCP is mutated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing size measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N-P.

claim: Crb fails to regulate the levels of Ex when the residue that is recognised by Slmb/β-TrCP is mutated.
source: Interestingly, expression of the S453A mutant version of Ex resulted in a more severe undergrowth than wt Ex, and this was refractory to Crbintra co-expression, suggesting that Crb fails to regulate the levels of Ex when the residue that is recognised by Slmb/β-TrCP is mutated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N–P).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the S453A mutant phenotype is not rescued by Crbintra.

claim: Expression of CkIα or Gish using hh-Gal4 resulted in a significant decrease in the levels of the ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporter in the posterior compartment.
source: Indeed, when compared to control wing discs, expression of CkIα or Gish using hh-Gal4 resulted in a significant decrease in the levels of the reporter in the posterior compartment (Figure 3H–3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3H-3K.

claim: Over-expression of either Dco or CG7094 did not affect ubi-Ex1-468::GFP levels in vivo.
source: However, this effect on Ex levels was not seen upon over-expression of either Dco or the poorly characterised CKI family member CG7094 (Figure 3K), indicating that not all CKIs modulate Ex stability in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Not all CKIs modulate Ex stability in vivo.
source: However, this effect on Ex levels was not seen upon over-expression of either Dco or the poorly characterised CKI family member CG7094 (Figure 3K), indicating that not all CKIs modulate Ex stability in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Dco and CG7094 overexpression do not affect Ex levels.

claim: The effect of CKIs on Ex is dependent on kinase activity.
source: Importantly, the effect of CKIs on Ex is not due to changes in Crb levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q), and is dependent on kinase activity, since a GishisoI kinase-deficient construct could not alter reporter levels (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The effect of CKIs on Ex is not due to changes in Crb levels.
source: Importantly, the effect of CKIs on Ex is not due to changes in Crb levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q), and is dependent on kinase activity, since a GishisoI kinase-deficient construct could not alter reporter levels (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: Over-expression of CKIs did not alter the levels of the S453A mutant reporter.
source: In contrast, over-expression of CKIs did not alter the levels of the S453A mutant reporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1R), providing further evidence that CKIs regulate Ex in a Slmb/β-TrCP-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1R.

claim: CKIs regulate Ex in a Slmb/β-TrCP-dependent manner.
source: In contrast, over-expression of CKIs did not alter the levels of the S453A mutant reporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1R), providing further evidence that CKIs regulate Ex in a Slmb/β-TrCP-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CKI overexpression does not affect the S453A mutant reporter.

claim: Upon treatment of S2 cells with gish RNAi, Crbintra-mediated depletion of both Ex1-468 and ExFL was strongly reduced.
source: Upon treatment of S2 cells with gish RNAi, Crbintra-mediated depletion of both Ex1-468 and ExFL was strongly reduced (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of ckIα or gish alone resulted in robust stabilisation of Ex1-468 in the presence of Crbintra.
source: In line with our previous data, knockdown of ckIα or gish alone resulted in robust stabilisation of Ex1-468 in the presence of Crbintra (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Depleting all CKIs resulted in a more prominent stabilisation of Ex1-468 than depleting individual CKIs.
source: It is noteworthy that depleting all CKIs resulted in a more prominent stabilisation of Ex1-468, suggesting that CkIα and Gish work together to regulate Ex stability (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CkIα and Gish work together to regulate Ex stability.
source: It is noteworthy that depleting all CKIs resulted in a more prominent stabilisation of Ex1-468, suggesting that CkIα and Gish work together to regulate Ex stability (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that depleting all CKIs has a stronger effect than depleting individual CKIs.

claim: The interaction between Ex and Slmb was abolished when gish or when all CKIs were depleted by RNAi.
source: Indeed, the interaction between Ex and Slmb was abolished when gish or when all CKIs were depleted by RNAi (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Crb-induced Ex ubiquitylation was dramatically reduced when gish or all CKIs were depleted by RNAi.
source: When we monitored Crb-induced Ex ubiquitylation, we observed that this was dramatically reduced when gish or all CKIs were depleted by RNAi (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Knocking-down CKIs had a similar effect to depletion of slmb on Ex ubiquitylation.
source: Indeed, knocking-down CKIs had a similar effect to depletion of slmb, part of the Ex E3 ligase complex activated downstream of Crb (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CKI kinases act downstream of Crb to promote the interaction of Ex with Slmb, thereby stimulating Ex ubiquitylation and degradation.
source: These data suggest that CKI kinases act downstream of Crb to promote the interaction of Ex with Slmb, thereby stimulating Ex ubiquitylation and degradation.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple experiments showing that CKI depletion blocks Crb-induced Ex:Slmb binding and ubiquitylation.

claim: Crb4A mut efficiently promoted Ex degradation similar to wt Crb.
source: Similar to wt Crb, Crb4A mut efficiently promoted Ex degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that aPKC phosphorylation is not required for the regulation of Ex downstream of Crb.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: aPKC phosphorylation is not required for the regulation of Ex downstream of Crb.
source: Similar to wt Crb, Crb4A mut efficiently promoted Ex degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that aPKC phosphorylation is not required for the regulation of Ex downstream of Crb.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Crb4A mut, which cannot be phosphorylated by aPKC, still promotes Ex degradation.

claim: Wts can stabilise ExFL.
source: Though our data confirm that Wts can stabilise ExFL, we observed that the presence of Wts did not prevent the degradation of Ex mediated by the expression of Crb, indicating that the N-terminal degron supersedes the C-terminal one when Crb triggers Ex degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The presence of Wts did not prevent the degradation of Ex mediated by the expression of Crb.
source: Though our data confirm that Wts can stabilise ExFL, we observed that the presence of Wts did not prevent the degradation of Ex mediated by the expression of Crb, indicating that the N-terminal degron supersedes the C-terminal one when Crb triggers Ex degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The N-terminal degron supersedes the C-terminal one when Crb triggers Ex degradation.
source: Though our data confirm that Wts can stabilise ExFL, we observed that the presence of Wts did not prevent the degradation of Ex mediated by the expression of Crb, indicating that the N-terminal degron supersedes the C-terminal one when Crb triggers Ex degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Wts stabilization of Ex is overridden by Crb-mediated degradation.

claim: No differences in ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporter levels were observed in third instar wing imaginal discs carrying clones mutant for gishKG03891 or dcole88 compared to control cells.
source: When we assessed the levels of the ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporter in third instar wing imaginal discs carrying clones mutant for existing gish (gishKG03891) or dco (dcole88) alleles, we observed no differences from control cells, suggesting that these kinases are not essential for maintaining Ex levels at steady state in vivo (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: gish and dco are not essential for maintaining Ex levels at steady state in vivo.
source: When we assessed the levels of the ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporter in third instar wing imaginal discs carrying clones mutant for existing gish (gishKG03891) or dco (dcole88) alleles, we observed no differences from control cells, suggesting that these kinases are not essential for maintaining Ex levels at steady state in vivo (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that gish and dco mutant clones do not show altered Ex reporter levels.

claim: Neither gish17 nor CG7094F2 mutant clones caused a change in ubi-Ex1-468::GFP levels compared to wt tissue.
source: However, when we generated FRT clones for these new alleles, neither caused a change in ubi-Ex1-468::GFP levels compared to wt tissue (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporter was elevated in ckIα8B12 clones.
source: In contrast, we observed that the ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporter was elevated in ckIα8B12 clones (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Apical levels of Crb were increased in ckIα8B12 clones.
source: We noticed that apical levels of Crb were also increased in ckIα8B12 clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The increase in Crb levels in ckIα8B12 clones was not due to a general increase in apical domain size.
source: This was not due to a general increase in apical domain size, since levels of another apical protein, aPKC, did not increase in ckIα8B12 clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Over-expression of Ex1-468 led to a robust increase in endogenous Crb at the apical membrane.
source: Indeed, over-expression of UAS-Ex1-468 led to a robust increase in endogenous Crb at the apical membrane (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Increased Crb levels were detected in slmb1 clones, albeit mainly when these clones were large.
source: However, upon careful examination, we were able to detect increased Crb levels in slmb1 clones, albeit mainly when these clones were large (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mutant clones for slmb9H4-17 displayed a clear increase in Crb levels.
source: Furthermore, mutant clones for a null allele, slmb9H4-17, displayed a clear increase in Crb levels (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Both slmb and ckIα mutant clones display elevated levels of Ex and Crb.
source: Thus, both slmb and ckIα mutant clones display elevated levels of Ex and Crb.
evidence: The claim is a summary of observations from imaging data shown in Figures 5C, 5E, 5F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Triple mutant clones lacking CG7094, gish and dco did not have altered levels of the Ex1-468::GFP reporter.
source: Since our S2 cell data suggested that several members of the CKI family may regulate Ex redundantly (Figure 4C), we generated triple mutant clones lacking CG7094, gish and dco, but these did not have altered levels of the Ex1-468::GFP reporter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Triple mutant clones for ckIα, gish and dco had elevated Ex and Crb levels.
source: Triple mutant clones for ckIα, gish and dco had elevated Ex and Crb levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I), but these were comparable to ckIα clones alone (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I.

claim: In vivo, it does not appear that CKI family members function redundantly to control Ex levels, at least in wing discs under normal developmental conditions.
source: Thus, in vivo, it does not appear that CKI family members function redundantly to control Ex levels, at least in wing discs under normal developmental conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that triple mutant clones for ckIα, gish and dco have similar phenotypes to ckIα clones alone.

claim: Loss of either slmb or ckIα led to a strong clone extrusion phenotype and a loss of ommatidial differentiation posterior to the morphogenetic furrow in the eye disc.
source: In the eye disc, loss of either slmb (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–A') or ckIα (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–D') led to a strong clone extrusion phenotype and a loss of ommatidial differentiation posterior to the morphogenetic furrow.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-A' and 2D-D'.

claim: Ex::GFP levels were elevated in both slmb or ckIα mutant clones in the leg and haltere discs.
source: In contrast, Ex::GFP levels were elevated in both slmb (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C') or ckIα (Figure 6E–6F') mutant clones in the leg and haltere discs.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-C' and Figure 6E-6F' (note: Figure 6E-6F' appears to be a typo and should likely refer to Figure 5—figure supplement 2E-F').

claim: The requirement for Slmb and CkIα to regulate Ex levels varies according to the tissue.
source: The requirement for Slmb and CkIα to regulate Ex levels therefore varies according to the tissue.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slmb and CkIα have different effects on Ex levels in different tissues.

claim: Expression of Crbintra caused depletion of all apical ubi-Ex1-468::GFP in the posterior compartment within 24 hr.
source: Expression of Crbintra caused depletion of all apical ubi-Ex1-468::GFP in the posterior compartment within 24 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of either ckIαRNAi or gishRNAi alone had little effect on ubi-Ex1-468::GFP expression in the posterior compartment.
source: Expression of either ckIαRNAi (Figure 6A–B) or gishRNAi (Figure 6E–F) alone had little effect on ubi-Ex1-468::GFP expression in the posterior compartment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6A-B, 6E-F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Co-expression of ckIαRNAi, but not gishRNAi, with Crbintra resulted in a significant rescue of levels and localisation of the ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporter compared to Crbintra alone.
source: However, co-expression of ckIαRNAi (Figure 6C–D), but not gishRNAi (Figure 6G–H), with Crbintra resulted in a significant rescue of levels and localisation of the ubi-Ex1-468::GFP reporter compared to Crbintra alone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6C-D, 6G-H, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: ckIα knockdown, but not gish knockdown, is able to inhibit Crb-mediated Ex degradation in vivo.
source: Thus, ckIα knockdown, but not gish knockdown, is able to inhibit Crb-mediated Ex degradation in vivo.
evidence: The claim is a summary of observations from imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6.

claim: dcoRNAi had no effect on Ex::GFP reporter levels in the absence or presence of Crbintra.
source: dcoRNAi had no effect on Ex::GFP reporter levels in the absence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), or presence of Crbintra (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Crbintra-expressing, GFP-marked MARCM clones caused complete loss of apical ubi-Ex1-468::mScarlet.
source: We confirmed these findings using the MARCM technique, and observed that Crbintra-expressing, GFP-marked MARCM clones caused complete loss of apical ubi-Ex1-468::mScarlet (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,G.

claim: gish MARCM clones expressing Crbintra resembled Crbintra MARCM clones alone (loss of the apical Ex reporter).
source: gish MARCM clones expressing Crbintra resembled Crbintra MARCM clones alone (loss of the apical Ex reporter) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Removing ckIα resulted in a partial rescue of Crb-induced Ex degradation, with a proportion of mutant cells retaining ubi-Ex1-468::mScarlet apically.
source: In contrast, removing ckIα resulted in a partial rescue of Crb-induced Ex degradation, with a proportion of mutant cells retaining ubi-Ex1-468::mScarlet apically (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: In vivo, CkIα regulates Ex stability by promoting Crb-induced turnover.
source: Together, these results suggest that, in vivo, CkIα regulates Ex stability by promoting Crb-induced turnover.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple in vivo experiments showing that CkIα depletion blocks Crb-induced Ex degradation.

claim: Levels of both ex-lacZ and diap1-GFP3.5 were markedly decreased in ckIα mutant wing disc clones.
source: Levels of both ex-lacZ and diap1-GFP3.5, a Yki-responsive fragment of the diap1 promoter (Zhang et al., 2008) were markedly decreased in ckIα mutant wing disc clones (Figure 7A,C), while ex-lacZ was not affected in gish mutant tissue (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A,C and cites a previous publication.

claim: ex-lacZ was not affected in gish mutant tissue.
source: Levels of both ex-lacZ and diap1-GFP3.5, a Yki-responsive fragment of the diap1 promoter (Zhang et al., 2008) were markedly decreased in ckIα mutant wing disc clones (Figure 7A,C), while ex-lacZ was not affected in gish mutant tissue (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Yki is excluded from the nucleus in ckIα mutant cells compared with neighbouring wild type tissue.
source: Furthermore, we used a Yki-GFP knock-in line (Fletcher et al., 2018) to show that Yki is excluded from the nucleus in ckIα mutant cells compared with neighbouring wild type tissue (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7D and cites a previous publication.

claim: Overexpression of CkIα, but not Gish, in the posterior compartment of the wing disc increased Yki activity as measured by ex-lacZ levels.
source: Finally, overexpression of CkIα, but not Gish, in the posterior compartment of the wing disc increased Yki activity as measured by ex-lacZ levels (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7E-H.

claim: Loss of ckIα leads to Ex stabilisation correlated with decreased Yki activity.
source: Thus, loss of ckIα leads to Ex stabilisation correlated with decreased Yki activity, while its overexpression has the opposite effect, consistent with a role for CkIα in promoting Yki activity via the control of Ex stability.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple experiments showing that ckIα loss decreases Yki activity and ckIα overexpression increases Yki activity.

claim: CkIα overexpression has the opposite effect (increased Yki activity) to ckIα loss.
source: Thus, loss of ckIα leads to Ex stabilisation correlated with decreased Yki activity, while its overexpression has the opposite effect, consistent with a role for CkIα in promoting Yki activity via the control of Ex stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7.

claim: CkIα promotes Yki activity via the control of Ex stability.
source: Thus, loss of ckIα leads to Ex stabilisation correlated with decreased Yki activity, while its overexpression has the opposite effect, consistent with a role for CkIα in promoting Yki activity via the control of Ex stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between CkIα effects on Ex stability and Yki activity.

claim: Ex is a key link between epithelial polarity and Hpo signalling.
source: Ex is a key link between epithelial polarity and Hpo signalling.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Crb recruits Ex to the apical membrane, where it can promote inhibition of Yki.
source: Via its FERM-binding motif (FBM), Crb recruits Ex to the apical membrane, where it can promote inhibition of Yki (Genevet and Tapon, 2011; Chen et al., 2010; Hafezi et al., 2012; Ling et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2010; Su et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field and cites previous publications.

claim: Crb stimulates Ex phosphorylation and turnover of Ex protein.
source: However, besides activating Hpo signalling through Ex, Crb also stimulates Ex phosphorylation and turnover of Ex protein (Genevet and Tapon, 2011; Grzeschik et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2010; Ling et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2010; Ribeiro et al., 2014; Laprise, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field and cites previous publications.

claim: Ubiquitylation and degradation of Ex downstream of Crb is mediated by the phospho-dependent SCFSlimb/β-TrCP E3 ligase complex.
source: We have previously shown that ubiquitylation and degradation of Ex downstream of Crb is mediated by the phospho-dependent SCFSlimb/β-TrCP E3 ligase complex, which is also thought to regulate Ex levels independently of Crb (Ribeiro et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous work and cites previous publications.

claim: The identity of the kinase(s) that promote Ex degradation downstream of Crb is currently unknown.
source: However, the identity of the kinase(s) that promote Ex degradation downstream of Crb is currently unknown.
evidence: The claim states the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The Casein Kinase 1 (CKI) family is required for Expanded phosphorylation.
source: Here, we show that the Casein Kinase 1 (CKI) family is required for Expanded phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments.

claim: CKI expression promotes Expanded phosphorylation and interaction with Slimb/β-TrCP.
source: CKI expression promotes Expanded phosphorylation and interaction with Slimb/β-TrCP.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings supported by multiple experiments in the study.

claim: CKI depletion in S2 cells impairs Expanded degradation downstream of Crumbs.
source: Conversely, CKI depletion in S2 cells impairs Expanded degradation downstream of Crumbs.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings supported by RNAi experiments in the study.

claim: In wing imaginal discs, CKI loss leads to elevated Expanded and Crumbs levels.
source: In wing imaginal discs, CKI loss leads to elevated Expanded and Crumbs levels.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings supported by in vivo experiments in the study.

claim: Phospho-dependent Expanded turnover ensures a tight coupling of Hippo pathway activity to epithelial architecture.
source: Thus, phospho-dependent Expanded turnover ensures a tight coupling of Hippo pathway activity to epithelial architecture.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion inferred from the findings of the study.

claim: CKI kinases regulate Ex in a partially redundant manner.
source: Interestingly, CKI kinases regulate Ex in a partially redundant manner, which suggests that regulation of Ex stability is a key step in the regulation of Yki function and the maintenance of tissue homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from S2 cell experiments showing that multiple CKIs can regulate Ex.

claim: Regulation of Ex stability is a key step in the regulation of Yki function and the maintenance of tissue homeostasis.
source: Interestingly, CKI kinases regulate Ex in a partially redundant manner, which suggests that regulation of Ex stability is a key step in the regulation of Yki function and the maintenance of tissue homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that multiple CKIs regulate Ex stability.

claim: Depletion of CKI kinases suppresses Crb-induced Ex phosphorylation, ubiquitylation and degradation.
source: Depletion of CKI kinases suppresses Crb-induced Ex phosphorylation, ubiquitylation and degradation.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings supported by RNAi experiments in the study.

claim: In cultured S2 cells, Gish (CKIγ) depletion has a strong effect on Ex stability.
source: An unexpected aspect of our results is the fact that, in cultured S2 cells, Gish (CKIγ) depletion has a strong effect on Ex stability (Figure 4A–C), while CkIα appears to be the dominant player in the wing imaginal disc, both in the presence (Figure 6C–D) and absence (Figure 5C) of Crbintra expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: CkIα appears to be the dominant player in the wing imaginal disc, both in the presence and absence of Crbintra expression.
source: An unexpected aspect of our results is the fact that, in cultured S2 cells, Gish (CKIγ) depletion has a strong effect on Ex stability (Figure 4A–C), while CkIα appears to be the dominant player in the wing imaginal disc, both in the presence (Figure 6C–D) and absence (Figure 5C) of Crbintra expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 6C-D and Figure 5C.

claim: Recruitment of CkIα to Crb/Ex may involve an adaptor protein expressed in the wing disc.
source: It is therefore possible that recruitment of CkIα to Crb/Ex may involve an adaptor protein expressed in the wing disc, as is the case for CkIε, which requires the DEAD-box RNA helicase DDX3 to phosphorylate Dishevelled2 in the mammalian Wnt pathway (Cruciat et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that CkIα is the dominant CKI in wing discs and by analogy to CkIε regulation, citing a previous publication.

claim: Yki activity is decreased upon ckIα depletion.
source: As Ex apical accumulation is predicted to antagonise Yki, we measured several readouts of Yki-dependent transcription and found that Yki activity is indeed decreased upon ckIα depletion and increased by CkIα overexpression, while Gish manipulations had no such effect (Figure 7A–C,E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-C,E-H.

claim: Yki activity is increased by CkIα overexpression.
source: As Ex apical accumulation is predicted to antagonise Yki, we measured several readouts of Yki-dependent transcription and found that Yki activity is indeed decreased upon ckIα depletion and increased by CkIα overexpression, while Gish manipulations had no such effect (Figure 7A–C,E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-C,E-H.

claim: Gish manipulations had no effect on Yki activity.
source: As Ex apical accumulation is predicted to antagonise Yki, we measured several readouts of Yki-dependent transcription and found that Yki activity is indeed decreased upon ckIα depletion and increased by CkIα overexpression, while Gish manipulations had no such effect (Figure 7A–C,E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-C,E-H.

claim: ckIα mutant clones are generally overgrown, round, and tend to delaminate from the wing disc epithelium.
source: However, we observed that ckIα mutant clones are generally overgrown, round, and tend to delaminate from the wing disc epithelium, so that they often do not contribute to the adult wing (Figure 5C and Figure 7A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 7A,C.

claim: The overgrowth phenotype of ckIα mutant clones is due to a strong elevation of Wingless (Wg) signalling in ckIα mutant tissue.
source: This overgrowth phenotype is due to a strong elevation of Wingless (Wg) signalling in ckIα mutant tissue (Legent et al., 2012) and is very similar to the loss of two Wg antagonists, axin and APC1/2 (Adenomatous Polyposis Coli) (Muñoz-Descalzo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications that have characterized the ckIα mutant phenotype.

claim: The decreased growth occurring as a result of partial loss of Yki activity in ckIα mutant clones is likely compensated by a strong increase in Wg signalling.
source: Thus, it is likely that the decreased growth occurring as a result of partial loss of Yki activity in ckIα mutant clones is compensated by a strong increase in Wg signalling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ckIα mutant clones are overgrown despite decreased Yki activity.

claim: Loss of either ckIα or slmb function results in an increase in the apical levels of Crb as well as Ex.
source: Our data also revealed that loss of either ckIα or slmb function results in an increase in the apical levels of Crb as well as Ex (Figure 5E–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Excess Ex accumulation leads to increased Crb apical levels.
source: Instead, we favour the second possibility, in which excess Ex accumulation leads to increased Crb apical levels. Consistent with this idea, over-expression of Ex1-468 leads to a robust increase in apical Crb (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Ex overexpression increases Crb levels, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Excess Ex interferes with Crb recognition by α-adaptin, thereby decreasing Crb internalisation rates in ckIα or slmb mutant clones.
source: It is therefore possible that excess Ex interferes with Crb recognition by α-adaptin, thereby decreasing Crb internalisation rates in ckIα or slmb mutant clones.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that Ex accumulation correlates with increased Crb levels and knowledge about Crb endocytosis.

claim: CRB3, the mammalian orthologue of Crb, can regulate Hippo signalling by mechanisms analogous to those described in Drosophila.
source: CRB3, the mammalian orthologue of Crb, can regulate Hippo signalling by mechanisms analogous to those described in Drosophila. CRB3 interacts with two proposed orthologues of Ex, Angiomotin (AMOT), and FRMD6, in a density-dependent manner (Varelas et al., 2010; Angus et al., 2012; Mao et al., 2018; Moleirinho et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field and cites previous publications.

claim: CRB3 interacts with two proposed orthologues of Ex, Angiomotin (AMOT), and FRMD6, in a density-dependent manner.
source: CRB3, the mammalian orthologue of Crb, can regulate Hippo signalling by mechanisms analogous to those described in Drosophila. CRB3 interacts with two proposed orthologues of Ex, Angiomotin (AMOT), and FRMD6, in a density-dependent manner (Varelas et al., 2010; Angus et al., 2012; Mao et al., 2018; Moleirinho et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field and cites previous publications.

claim: The apical polarity determinant Crb promotes Ex phosphorylation by CKI family kinases, which in turn stimulates Slmb/β-TrCP-mediated ubiquitylation and degradation.
source: In summary, our data support a model whereby the apical polarity determinant Crb promotes Ex phosphorylation by CKI family kinases, which in turn stimulates Slmb/β-TrCP-mediated ubiquitylation and degradation.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: This mechanism facilitates precise and dynamic control of Ex protein levels at the apical membrane, which is crucial for the regulation of Hippo signalling.
source: We propose that this mechanism facilitates precise and dynamic control of Ex protein levels at the apical membrane, which is crucial for the regulation of Hippo signalling.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion inferred from the findings of the study.
